documents.title: NavigateAI Use at CSU: What's allowed, When to ask, and What to avoid
documents.summary: A student-facing trail-map guide that sorts AI uses into three zones: always acceptable learning uses, uses that need the instructor's explicit permission, and uses that count as academic misconduct. The instructor decides what is allowed for credit work, and an FAQ section restates that help rules vary by course.
documents.stance_why: The page sets three tiers ("Some paths are open to everyone, some require special permits, and some are closed") and says "Using AI for any work you get credit for requires their explicit permission," with "Every guide runs their trail differently." The decision for graded work is handed to each instructor, so the document delegates and lists its tiers.

units.why: The opening sorts AI use into open, permit-required and closed paths: "Some paths are open to everyone, some require special permits, and some are closed". That is a named-tier scheme, so P05; it states no rule itself, so it informs.
units.anchor: Some paths are open to everyone, some require special permits, and some are closed
units.frag_start: Some paths are open to everyone,
units.resolution_why: Actor: A student, B all. The opening ('Welcome, Rams! ... your trail map') addresses students, so student. Both code P05 for the three zones (open, permit, closed).

units.why: Type: A P12, B P02. That is not a default-permit rule, so P12 (AI as tutor), with the fit note kept.
units.anchor: You are encouraged to use AI as your personal guide for learning and discovery.
units.fit_note: Encourages AI as a guide for learning and discovery in general, not only as a concept tutor. Encouragement applies only to the listed learning activities, not to graded work.
units.resolution_why: Type: A P12, B P02. units.anchor: Use AI to explain a complex topic from class in a new way.

They are one rule with its reason in the source ('Hiker's Wisdom'), so I kept A's single unit whose policy includes the reason and dropped B's separate warning unit.

P01, fit note kept; B's note merged.

units.why: "Write or co-author any part of a graded essay, lab report, or paper" is listed under uses to check with the instructor first. It is a writing-specific permission-required rule, so P18 (prose separate from code).

units.resolution_why: Type: A P22 (no AI on exams), B P04. The source lists take-home work as needing instructor permission; it is not a ban on assessments. P04, with the fit note kept.

units.anchor: The #1 Rule of the Trail: When in doubt, ask your guide.

units.why: "Turning in an essay, lab report, or any other assignment that was fully generated by an AI" is listed as misconduct. It is a ban on submitting AI-produced work, so P19.
units.anchor: any other assignment that was fully generated by an AI.

units.why: "Using an AI tool in any way to answer questions during a quiz or exam" is misconduct: a ban on AI in exams, so P22.
units.anchor: Using an AI tool in any way to answer questions during a quiz or exam.

units.why: "Including fake sources, data, or citations that an AI made up" is misconduct. It forbids submitting fabricated material that AI produced, which is closest to P74 (fabricate or falsify data); P31 only tells students to verify.
units.anchor: Including fake sources, data, or citations that an AI made up
units.fit_note: Concerns AI-fabricated sources in the student's own submission, not intent to deceive by the tool user in general.

units.why: "Using AI to rewrite or 'spin' sentences or paragraphs from a source and presenting them as your own original summary" is misconduct. AI is producing text submitted as one's own, so P19.

documents.summary: Faculty guide to writing short course AI statements, with four sample statements ranging from prohibitive to broadly permissive. It argues that a campus-wide umbrella policy is unlikely to fit and asks instructors to use their own judgment and update their statements.
documents.stance_why: The guide offers four adoptable sample statements and says "it seems unlikely that a campus umbrella policy will satisfy the many needs" and "You are urged to use your best judgment." It sets no university-wide AI rule and hands the decision to instructors, so it delegates with tiers.

units.anchor: they clarify expectations and help prevent misunderstanding
units.fit_note: Gives a reason for having statements rather than requiring them.
units.resolution_why: Found only by B. Source: 'They guide: they clarify expectations and help prevent misunderstanding.' This is a rationale for syllabus statements, which the codebook counts, so kept.

units.why: Type: A P09, B UNCOVERED; phase A course-start, B when-misuse. Source: statements 'exist for administrative reasons: ... they are what we point to as the stated expectation of the course and, then, justification for our intervention.' P09 is a duty to have a statement, and this sentence imposes none; it says what the statement is used for when misconduct occurs. UNCOVERED, phase when-misuse. A's fit note merged into the uncovered note.

documents.title: Policies & Resources (Academic Integrity section)
documents.summary: The department's student information guide lists behaviors that are clearly unacceptable in CS coursework, and one of them is turning in generative-AI work as one's own. No permitted AI uses are described.
documents.stance_why: The only AI text is a bullet under "Examples of clearly unacceptable behaviors": "Turning in work created by generative AI as one's own." It bans submitting AI-created work as one's own and names no allowed uses or instructor discretion, so the stance is prohibit for that work.

units.why: Under "Examples of clearly unacceptable behaviors" the department lists "Turning in work created by generative AI as one's own." That bans submitting AI-created work, so P19; it is also labelled unacceptable (P36), but the rule a reader would look for is the ban on submitting AI work.
units.anchor: Turning in work created by generative AI as one’s own.
units.policy: Turning in work created by generative AI as one's own is clearly unacceptable behavior in the CS Department.

notes: Reconciled from coder A and coder B. CS department page has a single AI bullet; its general integrity rules (must be able to explain your solution, penalties list, duty to report to the Office of Conflict Resolution and Student Conduct Services) do not mention AI and were not coded. Navigate AI page text repeats its three zones twice; repeats were coded once. Non-AI FAQ items (Course Hero, double submission, facilitation) were skipped. The navigate page's 'Undeclared use' line is coded P28. Coder B. The CS department page has one AI sentence; other academic-integrity text there (explain your solution, similarity) is not AI-specific and was not coded. The NavigateAI page repeats its text twice; coded once. The Course Hero and study-site FAQ was not coded (no AI content). Dropped units: B 'AI tools can sometimes lead you astray' (folded into the verification unit's policy text); B 'the expectation can change from course to course' (same sentence as the instructor-decides unit); A 'allowed to work with a partner at every step' (non-AI example); B 'create concise, effective ... syllabus statements' (statement of the guide's purpose, no rule); B 'you will receive significant guidance' (already in the limited-use policy text). Notes of dropped units: dropped A unit "allowed to work with a partner at every step of an assignment": Example is about partner collaboration, not AI. dropped B unit "the expectation can change from course to course": Stated for help on graded work in general, with a partner-work example, not only AI. dropped B unit "create concise, effective, and purpose-driven syllabus statements about the use of generative artificial intelligence": Offered as guidance to faculty, not as a mandate. dropped B unit "you will receive significant guidance on the appropriate use of such technologies": Promises guidance on assignments where AI is allowed rather than redesigning grading.
